arXiv:1812.07707v1 [math.AP] 19 Dec 2018

Convergence to the complex balanced equilibrium for some chemical reaction-diffusion systems with boundary equilibria

Gheorghe Craciun ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Department of Biomolecular Chemistry, University of Wisconsin-Madison, craciun@math.wisc.edu    Jiaxin Jin ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison jjin43@wisc.edu    Casian Pantea ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, West Virginia University, cpantea@math.wvu.edu    Adrian Tudorascu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, West Virginia University, adriant@math.wvu.edu
Abstract

In this paper we study the rate of convergence to the complex balanced equilibrium for some chemical reaction-diffusion systems with boundary equilibria. We first analyze a three-species system with boundary equilibria in some stoichiometric classes, and whose right hand side is bounded above by a quadratic nonlinearity in the positive orthant. We prove similar results on the convergence to the positive equilibrium for a fairly general two-species reversible reaction-diffusion network with boundary equilibria.

1 Introduction

The dynamical behavior of spatially homogeneous mass-action reaction systems has been the focus of much research over the last fifty years. These ODE systems are usually high-dimensional, non-linear, and depend on a large number of parameters, which makes them generally difficult to study. However, a fertile theory started fifty years ago with work of Horn, Jackson and Feinberg [20, 21, 15] has been successful in addressing questions of existence and stability of positive equilibria, and persistence (nonextinction) of variables. Their work shows that, surprisingly, the large class of complex balanced mass-action systems have unique positive equilibria and admit a global Lyapunov function, which makes them locally asymptotically stable independently of reaction rate constant values. This robustness is relevant in applications, where exact values of system parameters are typically unknown. Moreover, Horn conjectured that the unique equilibria are in fact globally asymptotically stable [21], a question known as the Global Attractor Conjecture. The conjecture stayed open until recent years, when new work fueled in part by advances in systems biology led to a series of partial results. It was shown that trajectories of complex balanced systems either converge to the positive equilibrium or go to boundary equilibria [28, 29], establishing that persistence implies global stability. A series of subsequent papers showed persistence for complex balanced systems in two variables and other classes of systems, and proved the Global Attractor Conjecture in two and three variables [1, 7, 2, 3, 25, 8, 19, 19]. This work led to a very recent proof of the Global Attractor Conjecture in full generality by Craciun [9].

Much less is known about the corresponding reaction-diffusion models, although a number of recent papers have focused on extending the results above in the PDE setting. A promising venue for relating the PDE and ODE models is by way of space discretization (the method of lines). As proof of concept, the network A+B⇌CA+B\rightleftharpoons C was considered in [24] where it was shown that solutions of the discretized system converge to the solution of the PDE system as the space discretization grows finer. Solutions of the reaction-diffusion system A+B⇌CA+B\rightleftharpoons C have been shown to approach a positive spatially homogeneous distribution [27] via semigroup theory. Newer work uses entropy techniques to prove global asymptotic stability for other systems, including dimerization networks 2​A⇌B2A\rightleftharpoons B [10] and monomolecular networks [16].

For general complex balanced systems it was shown that under the assumption of equal diffusion constants, their ω\omega-limit set consists of constant functions corresponding to equilibria of the space-homogeneous ODE system and that, moreover, the unique positive equilibrium is asymptotically stable. This is the analogous of the “persistence implies global stability” result from the ODE setting, albeit in the case of equal diffusion constants. Recent results by Desvillettes, Fellner and collaborators [12, 14] removed the requirement of equal diffusion constants, and showed that in the absence of boundary equilibria, the positive equilibrium of general complex balanced reaction-diffusion systems attracts all solutions with positive initial data. These papers also considered special cases of networks with boundary equilibria, where a more detailed analysis showed that positive solutions remain globally asymptotically stable. However, the general case of systems with boundary equilibria remains open, and the analysis of such systems is on a case-by-case basis.

Our paper studies two cases of complex balanced reaction networks with boundary equilibria, and shows that under mild boundedness conditions on the initial data, solutions converge asymptotically to the unique positive equilibria. Namely, we consider the three-species system A+n​B⇌B+CA+nB{\rightleftharpoons}B+C (Theorem 1.1), and the two-species system m1​A+n1​B⇌m2​A+n2​Bm_{1}A+n_{1}B{\rightleftharpoons}m_{2}A+n_{2}B (Theorem 1.2).

In the remainder of this introductory section we set up terminology and notation, we discuss some of the techniques used here and in previous work, and we state our main theorems. Sections 2 and 3 contain the proofs of the results for the three-species and two-species systems. We conclude with a few remarks and open problems (Section 4) and with an appendix collecting a few technical results needed in the paper.

1.1 Terminology and previous results

Let us consider 0<T≤∞0<T\leq\infty and the semilinear parabolic system

𝐜t−𝒟​Δ​𝐜=R⁡(𝐜)​ in ​Ω×(0,T),𝐜⁡(⋅,0)=𝐜0​ in ​Ω,\mathbf{c}_{t}-\mathcal{D}\Delta\mathbf{c}=R(\mathbf{c})\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\ \mathbf{c}(\cdot,0)=\mathbf{c}_{0}\mbox{ in }\Omega, (1)

where 𝐜:Ω×[0,T)→ℝn\mathbf{c}:\Omega\times[0,T)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} is the vector of concentrations at spatial position x∈Ωx\in\Omega (an open subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}) and time t∈[0,∞)t\in[0,\infty), 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a positive definite, diagonal n×nn\times n matrix, and R:ℝn→ℝnR:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n} is a vector field whose components are polynomials (determined by the chemical reactions under consideration). This system can be linear and “trivial” (at least in the sense that “enough” of its equations decouple), such as

at−da​Δ​a=−k​a,bt−db​Δ​b=k​a​ in ​Ω×(0,T),a(⋅,0)=a0,b(⋅,0)=b0 in Ω,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=-ka,\\ \displaystyle b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=ka\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \displaystyle a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0}\mbox{ in }\Omega,\end{array}

(which corresponds to the reaction A→BA\displaystyle\rightarrow B with reaction rate k>0k>0), linear and nontrivial (weakly coupled) such as

at−da​Δ​a=−k1​a+k2​b,bt−db​Δ​b=k1​a−k2​b​ in ​Ω×(0,T),a(⋅,0)=a0,b(⋅,0)=b0 in Ω,\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=-k_{1}a+k_{2}b,\\ \displaystyle b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=k_{1}a-k_{2}b\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \displaystyle a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0}\mbox{ in }\Omega,\end{array}

(which corresponds to A​⇌k2k1​BA\overset{k_{1}}{\underset{k_{2}}{\rightleftharpoons}}B). However, as soon as a reaction includes two or more reactants, the system becomes nonlinear in the zero order terms (semilinear). For example, the single reaction A+B​→𝑘​CA+B\overset{k}{\rightarrow}C yields

at−da​Δ​a=−k​a​b,bt−db​Δ​b=−k​a​b,ct−dc​Δ​c=k​a​b​ in ​Ω×(0,T)a(⋅,0)=a0,b(⋅,0)=b0,c(⋅,0)=c0 in Ω.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=-kab,\\ \displaystyle b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=-kab,\\ \displaystyle c_{t}-d_{c}\Delta c=kab\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T)\\ \displaystyle a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0},\ c(\cdot,0)=c_{0}\mbox{ in }\Omega.\end{array}

We use this last system to illustrate some terminology and notation. Here A,B,A,\ B, and CC are the three species of the network, and A+BA+B and CC are its complexes. In general, complexes are formal linear combinations of species with non-negative integer coefficients, and sit on both sides of a reaction arrow. It is useful to think of complexes as vectors in a natural way, for example A+BA+B corresponds to y=(1,1,0)y=(1,1,0), and CC to y′=(0,0,1)y^{\prime}=(0,0,1). The concentrations of A,B,CA,\ B,\ C are non-negative functions of time and space and are collected in the concentration vector 𝐜=(a,b,c)\mathbf{c}=(a,b,c). The reaction rate of a reaction is given by mass-action, and is proportional to the concentration of each reactant species. This way, the reaction A+B​→𝑘​CA+B\overset{k}{\rightarrow}C has rate k​a​bkab. The reaction rate constant kk is a reaction-specific positive number. In general, the rate of a the reaction y​→𝑘​y′y\overset{k}{\to}y^{\prime} is given by

k​𝐜y=k​∏i=1nciyi,k\mathbf{c}^{y}=k\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{y_{i}},

where nn is the number of species, and complexes yy and y′y^{\prime} are viewed as vectors, as illustrated above. The reaction rate k​a​bkab enters with negative sign in the equations for ata_{t} and btb_{t} (AA and BB are being consumed in the reaction), and with positive sign in the equation for ctc_{t} (CC is being produced). The aggregate contribution of all reaction rates are collected in the vector R⁡(𝐜)=(−k​a​b,−k​a​b,k​a​b)R(\mathbf{c})=(-kab,-kab,kab). In general, this is given by

R⁡(𝐜):=∑y→y′ky→y′​𝐜y​(y′−y),R(\mathbf{c}):=\sum_{y\to y^{\prime}}k_{y\to y^{\prime}}\mathbf{c}^{y}(y^{\prime}-y),

where ky→y′k_{y\to y^{\prime}} is the rate constant of y→y′y\to y^{\prime} and the summation is over all reactions y→y′y\to y^{\prime} in the network. Finally, 𝒟=diag⁡{da,db,dc}∈M3×3​(ℝ)\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{diag}\{d_{a},d_{b},d_{c}\}\in M_{3\times 3}(\mathbb{R}) denotes the diagonal matrix of diffusion constants.

In the previous example the first two equations have the benefit of being decoupled, but that feature is lost as soon as we allow for reversibility; indeed, corresponding to A+B​⇌k2k1​CA+B\overset{k_{1}}{\underset{k_{2}}{\rightleftharpoons}}C we have

at−da​Δ​a=−k1​a​b+k2​c,bt−db​Δ​b=−k1​a​b+k2​c,ct−dc​Δ​c=k1​a​b−k2​c​ in ​Ω×(0,T)a(⋅,0)=a0,b(⋅,0)=b0,c(⋅,0)=c0 in Ω.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=-k_{1}ab+k_{2}c,\\ \displaystyle b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=-k_{1}ab+k_{2}c,\\ \displaystyle c_{t}-d_{c}\Delta c=k_{1}ab-k_{2}c\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,T)\\ \displaystyle a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0},\ c(\cdot,0)=c_{0}\mbox{ in }\Omega.\end{array} (2)

When it comes to basic questions on the existence, uniqueness, smoothness and non-negativity of solutions (if the initial data components are nonnegative), for linear systems the answers are provided in the (by now, classical) literature (see, e.g., [26]). However, complexity adds quickly as more reactions and/or more reactants enter the system. There is no general result in the literature that guarantees long time existence, uniqueness and non-negativity of solutions, let alone smoothness and other, more delicate properties such as comparison principles and convergence to equilibrium. In this paper we discuss chemical reaction diffusion systems which have a specific structure relative to a positive equilibrium, i.e. a steady state solution with all positive components.

In general, we say that an equilibrium point c0c_{0} is a complex balanced equilibrium if for all complexes y¯\bar{y} we have

∑y¯→yky¯→y​c0y¯=∑y→y¯ky→y¯​c0y\sum_{\bar{y}\to y}k_{\bar{y}\to y}c_{0}^{\bar{y}}=\sum_{y\to\bar{y}}k_{y\to\bar{y}}c_{0}^{y}

i.e., the total chemical flux that exits the complex y¯\bar{y} equals the total chemical flux that enters the complex y¯\bar{y} (for any choice of y¯\bar{y}). A chemical system is called a complex balanced system if it admits a positive complex balanced equilibrium. Due to the particular polynomial nature of R⁡(𝐜)R(\mathbf{c}) in this case, the steady states are all constant vectors (i.e. independent of location, as well as of time). If at least one component of a steady state is null, then the corresponding state is said to be a boundary equilibrium. All systems arising from complex balanced CRDSs admit a “canonical” Lyapunov functional of the relative Boltzmann entropy type. Its general form (again, see, e.g., [14]), this logarithmic free relative energy functional reads

E⁡(t):=∑i=1n∫Ω[ci​(x,t)​log⁡ci​(x,t)ci,∞−ci​(x,t)+ci,∞]​𝑑x,E(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{\Omega}\bigg[c_{i}(x,t)\log\frac{c_{i}(x,t)}{c_{i,\infty}}-c_{i}(x,t)+c_{i,\infty}\bigg]dx,

where 𝐜∞:=(c1,∞,…,cn,∞)\mathbf{c}_{\infty}:=(c_{1,\infty},...,c_{n,\infty}) is the constant vector denoting the positive complex balanced equilibrium. The entropy dissipation functional is computed by differentiating EE along trajectories; that is, once all the time derivatives of concentrations are replaced by their equation specific expressions and the Neumann BC are used to integrate by parts wherever the Laplacian appears, one gets

D⁡(t):=∑i=1ndi​∫Ω|∇ci​(x,t)|2ci​(x,t)​𝑑x+∑r=1ρkr​c∞yr​∫ΩΦ⁡(cyrc∞yr,cyr′c∞yr′)​𝑑x,D(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}\int_{\Omega}\frac{|\nabla c_{i}(x,t)|^{2}}{c_{i}(x,t)}dx+\sum_{r=1}^{\rho}k_{r}c_{\infty}^{y_{r}}\int_{\Omega}\Phi\bigg(\frac{c^{y_{r}}}{c_{\infty}^{y_{r}}};\frac{c^{y^{\prime}_{r}}}{c_{\infty}^{y^{\prime}_{r}}}\bigg)dx,

where ρ\rho is the number of reactions and Φ⁡(x,y):=x​log⁡(x/y)−x+y\Phi(x,y):=x\log(x/y)-x+y. Of course, one gets exponential decay to zero for EE if one can prove that there exists a positive constant α\alpha such that

D⁡(t)≥α​E​(t)​ for all ​t≥0.D(t)\geq\alpha E(t)\mbox{ for all }t\geq 0. (3)

Naturally, E⁡(t)E(t) should not only be identically zero when 𝐜⁡(t)=𝐜∞\mathbf{c}(t)=\mathbf{c}_{\infty}, but it should also be bounded below by some increasing function of the distance (from some norm) between 𝐜⁡(t)\mathbf{c}(t) and 𝐜∞\mathbf{c}_{\infty}.

For complex balanced systems, in the spatially isotropic case (𝒟=0\mathcal{D}=0, so the PDE’s are reduced to ODE’s) there is some recent work by Craciun [9], which answers in the affirmative a long standing conjecture on the convergence to the positive equilibrium in each stoichiometric class, called the Global Attractor Conjecture. This conjecture states that regardless of the existence of boundary equilibria, trajectories starting in the positive orthant converge to the unique positive equilibrium in the corresponding stoichiometric class. In the PDE case, the most general result concerns the case where there are no boundary equilibria. Very recently, Desvillettes, Fellner and Tang [14] showed that, contingent on the existence of suitable solutions (essentially, solutions that may not be classical but they are renormalized and do satisfy a weak entropy entropy-dissipation law), one obtains exponentially fast convergence to the equilibrium which lies in the same stoichiometric class as the initial data, which is merely assumed nonnegative and integrable over some bounded, C2C^{2} domain in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This is also a remarkably general result in the sense that the initial concentrations are only assumed to lie in L1​(Ω)L^{1}(\Omega). This improvement (over the previous works, where L∞L^{\infty}-bounds were imposed on the initial data) is achieved via the use of the Log-Sobolev inequality (see, e.g., [14]) in order to establish the entropy-entropy dissipation inequality (EEDI) (3). In all the previous works, the EEDI follows from the standard zero-average Poincaré inequality applied to the square roots of the concentration functions, combined with their uniform L∞L^{\infty}-bounds (in space-time); these bounds need to be proved a priori. This uniform L∞L^{\infty}-bound is key to the proofs of convergence to equilibrium in most of the works on this topic, (in fact, to our knowledge, the only exception comes when there are no boundary equilibria [14]) and the constant α\alpha from the EEDI (3) tends to vanish as the L∞L^{\infty}-bound on the solution blows up. We note that (2) is one of the two systems studied in [10], and the authors use the uniform L∞L^{\infty}-bound as available in the literature (for this particular system). In [24] the authors carry out the proof in some detail (adapted from a proof in [5]), and show that the properties of the Neumann Heat Kernel involved in it hold for the discrete Neumann Heat Kernel as well; as a consequence, one can emulate the proof in the continuous case to obtain uniform L∞L^{\infty} bounds for the discretized problem. The main idea of the proof is a bootstrapping argument in which the bounds obtained on aa and bb in terms of cc (from the first two equations of (2) we get at−ka​Δ​a≤k2​ca_{t}-k_{a}\Delta a\leq k_{2}c and bt−kb​Δ​b≤k2​cb_{t}-k_{b}\Delta b\leq k_{2}c) are fed into the inequality ct−kc​Δ​c≤k1​a​bc_{t}-k_{c}\Delta c\leq k_{1}ab (from the third equation of (2)) to yield an L∞L^{\infty} bound on cc at some time t≥δ>0t\geq\delta>0 in terms of a sublinear function of the bound at times t≤δ/2t\leq\delta/2. The success of this method relies on the right hand sides of the first two equations of (2) being bounded above in the positive orthant by a constant multiple of cc. It therefore fails for systems with all multiple-species complexes (no single species in any complex) or systems where single species appear more than once in any given complex (such as A+B⇌2​CA+B{\rightleftharpoons}2C). These bounds are crucial to the proof of consistency and, ultimately, convergence [24].

Our method to prove these uniform L∞L^{\infty} bounds seems confined to one-D, as it uses the stronger form of Poincaré’s inequality on a bounded interval (where the essential sup norm of a Sobolev function is bounded in terms of its average and the L1L^{1} norm of its Sobolev derivative). This leads to a uniform estimate (with respect to tt) of the L2L^{2} norm of the solutions in cylinders of type (t,t+1)×(0,1)(t,t+1)\times(0,1), which, once more using d=1d=1, leads to a uniform in time L∞L^{\infty} bound in the case where one of the right hand side polynomials is bounded above by a quadratic polynomial. It is an important improvement that we can deal with the at most quadratic case, since previous results (when boundary equilibria are present) only dealt with two species reactions or, if at least three species are present, the right hand side of an equation from the system is dominated by a first-degree polynomial [10], [11], [12], [13], [16] etc.

1.2 The three-species system.

A case not covered so far in the literature is A+n​B⇌B+CA+nB{\rightleftharpoons}B+C (n≥2n\geq 2 is an integer); this has boundary equilibria in some (not all) stoichiometric classes, translates to a 3×33\times 3 system (2×22\times 2 being, in general, easier to treat via the standard maximum principle for the heat equation), and the right hand side is not bounded above (in the positive orthant) by a linear term. More precisely, the PDE system we are looking at is

{at−da​Δ​a=−k1​a​bn+k2​b​cbt−db​Δ​b=−k1​a​bn+k2​b​c in ​Ω×(0,∞)ct−dc​Δ​c=k1​a​bn−k2​b​c∇a⋅ν=∇b⋅ν=∇c⋅ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,∞)a⁡(⋅,0)=a0,b⁡(⋅,0)=b0,c⁡(⋅,0)=c0 in ​Ω,\begin{cases}a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=-k_{1}ab^{n}+k_{2}bc&\\ b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=-k_{1}ab^{n}+k_{2}bc&\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ c_{t}-d_{c}\Delta c=k_{1}ab^{n}-k_{2}bc&\\ \nabla{a}\cdot\nu=\nabla{b}\cdot\nu=\nabla{c}\cdot\nu=0&\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0},\ c(\cdot,0)=c_{0}&\mbox{ in }\Omega,\end{cases}

where ν\nu is the (outward) normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Notice that by rescaling time tt, space xx and the concentrations (a,b,c)(a,b,c), we can always assume that the reaction rates and the domain volume are 1; to fix ideas, let us choose, without loss of generality, n=2n=2 and k1=k2=1k_{1}=k_{2}=1. The only important restriction we impose is the choice of spatial dimension d=1d=1. This is necessary due to the uniform L∞L^{\infty} bound on the solution, which is crucial to our analysis and we can (for the time being) only justify in the d=1d=1 case; that is, only the estimates in subsection 2.1 are predicated on this restriction. Therefore, the 3×33\times 3 reaction-diffusion system considered here is

{at−da​ax​x=−a​b2+b​cbt−db​bx​x=−a​b2+b​c in ​(0,1)×(0,∞)ct−dc​cx​x=a​b2−b​cax=bx=cx=0 on ​{0,1}×(0,∞)a⁡(⋅,0)=a0,b⁡(⋅,0)=b0,c⁡(⋅,0)=c0 in ​(0,1).\begin{cases}a_{t}-d_{a}a_{xx}=-ab^{2}+bc&\\ b_{t}-d_{b}b_{xx}=-ab^{2}+bc&\mbox{ in }(0,1)\times(0,\infty)\\ c_{t}-d_{c}c_{xx}=ab^{2}-bc&\\ a_{x}=b_{x}=c_{x}=0&\mbox{ on }\{0,1\}\times(0,\infty)\\ a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0},\ c(\cdot,0)=c_{0}&\mbox{ in }(0,1).\end{cases} (4)

The conserved (in time) quantities here are a¯+c¯\bar{a}+\bar{c} and b¯+c¯\bar{b}+\bar{c}, where f¯\bar{f} denotes the average of the function ff over Ω\Omega. If b∞>0b_{\infty}>0 we obviously can only have a boundary equilibrium at (0,b∞,0)(0,b_{\infty},0) (i.e. a∞=c∞=0a_{\infty}=c_{\infty}=0). The conservation of a¯+c¯\bar{a}+\bar{c} forces a≡c≡0a\equiv c\equiv 0, the second equation of the system decouples into bt−db​bx​x=0b_{t}-d_{b}b_{xx}=0, and b∞=b¯0b_{\infty}=\bar{b}_{0}. This steady state cannot be approached from any initial state for which a¯0+c¯0>0\bar{a}_{0}+\bar{c}_{0}>0, so no initial data in the positive orthant will converge to it. The other nontrivial type of steady states is given by b∞=0b_{\infty}=0 and a∞+c∞=a¯0+c¯0>0a_{\infty}+c_{\infty}=\bar{a}_{0}+\bar{c}_{0}>0. If c∞=0c_{\infty}=0, we get b≡c≡0b\equiv c\equiv 0 (from the conservation of b¯+c¯\bar{b}+\bar{c}), so, once again, an equilibrium of the type (a∞,0,0)(a_{\infty},0,0) cannot be approached from the positive orthant. We are left with the case (a∞,0,c∞)(a_{\infty},0,c_{\infty}) for a∞​c∞>0a_{\infty}c_{\infty}>0. We do not know how to prove that a¯0​b¯0​c¯0>0\bar{a}_{0}\bar{b}_{0}\bar{c}_{0}>0 prevents convergence to such steady states, but in this paper we will prove a weaker statement, namely:

Theorem 1.1.

If a0,b0,c0∈L∞​(0,1)a_{0},\ b_{0},c_{0}\in L^{\infty}(0,1) are a.e. nonnegative and such that a¯0​b¯0​c¯0>0\bar{a}_{0}\bar{b}_{0}\bar{c}_{0}>0 and b0≥δb_{0}\geq\delta a.e. in (0,1)(0,1) for some δ>0\delta>0, then the (unique) global classical solution to (4) converges asymptotically exponentially fast (at an explicit rate) to the unique positive equilibrium in its stoichiometric class.

The above theorem will be proved in Section 2.

1.3 The two-species system

Finally, in Section 3 we prove similar results on the convergence to the positive equilibrium for a two-species reversible reaction-diffusion network with boundary equilibria:

m1​A+n1​B⇌m2​A+n2​B.m_{1}A+n_{1}B{\rightleftharpoons}m_{2}A+n_{2}B.

Assume m1>m2>0m_{1}>m_{2}>0 and 0<n1<n20<n_{1}<n_{2} with m¯=m1−m2\bar{m}=m_{1}-m_{2}, n¯=n2−n1\bar{n}=n_{2}-n_{1} and m¯<n¯\bar{m}<\bar{n}. The 2×22\times 2 reaction-diffusion system is

{at−da​Δ​a=m¯​(am2​bn2−am1​bn1) in ​Ω×(0,∞)bt−db​Δ​b=n¯​(am1​bn1−am2​bn2) in ​Ω×(0,∞)∇a⋅ν=∇b⋅ν=0 on ​∂Ω×(0,∞)a⁡(⋅,0)=a0,b⁡(⋅,0)=b0 in ​Ω.\begin{cases}a_{t}-d_{a}\Delta a=\bar{m}(a^{m_{2}}b^{n_{2}}-a^{m_{1}}b^{n_{1}})&\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ b_{t}-d_{b}\Delta b=\bar{n}(a^{m_{1}}b^{n_{1}}-a^{m_{2}}b^{n_{2}})&\mbox{ in }\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ \nabla{a}\cdot\nu=\nabla{b}\cdot\nu=0&\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega\times(0,\infty)\\ a(\cdot,0)=a_{0},\ b(\cdot,0)=b_{0}&\mbox{ in }\Omega.\end{cases} (5)
Theorem 1.2.

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with a smooth boundary, for some integer d≥1d\geq 1. If 0<α≤a0​(x),b0​(x)≤β<+∞0<\alpha\leq a_{0}(x),b_{0}(x)\leq\beta<+\infty for a.e. xx in Ω\Omega, then the (unique) global classical solution to (5) converges asymptotically exponentially (at an explicit rate) to the unique positive equilibrium in its stoichiometric class.

2 Asymptotic decay for the three-species system

We consider the entropy functional E⁡(a,b,c)E(a,b,c) and the corresponding entropy dissipation (when computed along solutions) D⁡(a,b,c)=−dd​t​E​(a,b,c)D(a,b,c)=-\frac{d}{dt}{E(a,b,c)} associated to the system:

and

D⁡(a,b,c)=4​da​∫01|∂xa|2​𝑑x+4​db​∫01|∂xb|2​𝑑x+4​dc​∫01|∂xc|2​𝑑x+∫01(ab2−bc)ln⁡(a​b2b​c)dx.\begin{split}&D(a,b,c)=4d_{a}\int_{0}^{1}{|\partial_{x}{\sqrt{a}}|^{2}}dx+4d_{b}\int_{0}^{1}{|\partial_{x}{\sqrt{b}}|^{2}}dx+4d_{c}\int_{0}^{1}{|\partial_{x}{\sqrt{c}}|^{2}}dx\\ &+\int_{0}^{1}{(ab^{2}-bc)\ln(\frac{ab^2}{bc})dx}.\end{split} (7)

We would also like to record (for later use) the following conservation laws

∫01a⁡(x,t)​dx+∫01c⁡(x,t)​dx=∫01a0​(x)​dx+∫01c0​(x)​dx=:M1,∫01b⁡(x,t)​dx+∫01c⁡(x,t)​dx=∫01b0​(x)​dx+∫01c0​(x)​dx=:M2,\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{1}a(x,t)dx+\int_{0}^{1}c(x,t)dx=\int_{0}^{1}a_{0}(x)dx+\int_{0}^{1}c_{0}(x)dx=:M_{1},\\ &\int_{0}^{1}b(x,t)dx+\int_{0}^{1}c(x,t)dx=\int_{0}^{1}b_{0}(x)dx+\int_{0}^{1}c_{0}(x)dx=:M_{2},\end{split} (8)

for all t≥0t\geq 0. Note that these are simply obtained by adding equations 1 and 3 (respectively, 2 and 3) and integrating in space over [0,1][0,1] by taking into account the boundary conditions. 2.2 Uniform L∞L^{\infty} estimate

In this section we shall prove that a classical solution to (4) is bounded uniformly in time (and therefore, it also exists for all time). To achieve this, our goal is to place ourselves in the setting of Theorem 4.1 [17]. We shall refrain from transcribing the assumptions (H1)–(H3) from [17] here, as they are universally satisfied by CRDN systems with nonnegative and essentially bounded initial conditions. On the other hand, assumption (H4’) is both specific to our case and nontrivial to verify. We state it below, as it refers to a general semilinear parabolic m×mm\times m system

ui,t−κiΔui=fi(x,t,u),i=1,…,m,u_{i,t}-\kappa_{i}\Delta u_{i}=f_{i}(x,t,u),\ i=1,...,m, (10)

where x∈Ωx\in\Omega, t>0t>0, u=(u1,…,um)u=(u_{1},...,u_{m}). It reads:

 There exist ​K1,K2>0, 1≤p<∞, 1≤r<1+[1−dp⁡(d+2)]​2​pd+2​ such that \mbox{ There exist }K_{1},\ K_{2}>0,\ 1\leq p<\infty,\ 1\leq r<1+\bigg[1-\frac{d}{p(d+2)}\bigg]\frac{2p}{d+2}\mbox{ such that }
 for each ​1≤j≤m​ there exist ​αj,k, 1≤j≤k​ with ​αj,j=1​ such that \mbox{ for each }1\leq j\leq m\mbox{ there exist }\alpha_{j,k},\ 1\leq j\leq k\mbox{ with }\alpha_{j,j}=1\mbox{ such that } (11)
∑k=1jαj,k​fj​(x,t,v)≤K1​|v|r+K2​ for all ​v​ in the positive orthant of ​ℝm.\sum_{k=1}^{j}\alpha_{j,k}f_{j}(x,t,v)\leq K_{1}|v|^{r}+K_{2}\mbox{ for all }v\mbox{ in the positive orthant of }\mathbb{R}^{m}.

The following result is a version of Theorem 4.1 [17].

Theorem 2.2.

Suppose the initial data uj,0∈L∞​(Ω)u_{j,0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega), j=1,…,mj=1,...,m, the generic assumptions (H1)–(H3) from [17] hold. Further assume (11) holds for some 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty and

‖u‖Lp​(Ω×(τ,τ+1),ℝm)≤M<∞​ for all ​τ≥0.\|u\|_{L^{p}(\Omega\times(\tau,\tau+1);\mathbb{R}^{m})}\leq M<\infty\mbox{ for all }\tau\geq 0. (12)

Then

u∈L∞​(Ω×[0,∞),ℝm).u\in L^{\infty}(\Omega\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^{m}). (13)

A word of caution is in order: in [17] the analysis is performed on the whole space Ω=ℝd\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{d} and for more general elliptic operators (instead of the Laplacian). However, we argue that Theorem 2.2 holds for bounded domains Ω\Omega as well. Indeed, our elliptic operator is the Laplacian and on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} we have that the estimate (used to prove Lemma 2.1 in [17]) on the fundamental solution to the corresponding parabolic operator

0<G(x,ξ,t,τ)≤c1(T)(t−τ)−d/2exp{−|x−ξ|2c2​(T)​(t−τ)}0<G(x,\xi,t,\tau)\leq c_{1}(T)(t-\tau)^{-d/2}\exp\{-\frac{|x-\xi|^{2}}{c_{2}(T)(t-\tau)}\bigg\}

for x,ξ∈Ω, 0<τ<t≤T<∞x,\ \xi\in\Omega,\ 0<\tau<t\leq T<\infty (where c1​(T),c2​(T)c_{1}(T),\ c_{2}(T) are bounded for finite TT) holds for the Heat Kernel with Neumann BC on a bounded domain as well (see, e.g, [6]) with c1​(t)=c​etc_{1}(t)=ce^{t}, and c2​(t)=Cc_{2}(t)=C, for some constants c,C>0c,\ C>0. Likewise, for the homogeneous problem with initial value at T≥0T\geq 0, we also have the estimate

0<GT(x,ξ,t)≤c1(t−T)(t−T)−d/2exp{−|x−ξ|2c2​(t−T)​(t−T)},0<G_{T}(x,\xi,t)\leq c_{1}(t-T)(t-T)^{-d/2}\exp\{-\frac{|x-\xi|^{2}}{c_{2}(t-T)(t-T)}\bigg\},

which is used to prove Lemma 4.1 [17]. In the proof of Lemma 2.2 [17] there is an estimate on solutions of the adjoint equation; [22] is given as a reference. We limit ourselves to noting that [22] covers the case of and provides the same estimate on bounded domains as well. These are the estimates one needs to check in order to convince oneself that Theorem 2.2 holds on a bounded domain Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset{R}^{d}.

If we go back to (4) and denote by

u:=(a,b,c),f:=(−a​b2+b​c,−a​b2+b​c,a​b2−b​c)u:=(a,b,c),\ f:=(-ab^{2}+bc,-ab^{2}+bc,ab^{2}-bc)

we see that (11) is satisfied with α1,1=1,α2,1=−1,α2,2=1,α3,1=0,α3,2=−1,α3,3=1\alpha_{1,1}=1,\alpha_{2,1}=-1,\ \alpha_{2,2}=1,\ \alpha_{3,1}=0,\ \alpha_{3,2}=-1,\ \alpha_{3,3}=1, r=2r=2, K1=k2/2K_{1}=k_{2}/2, K2=0K_{2}=0. Theorem 2.3.

If a0,b0,c0∈L∞​(Ω)a_{0},\ b_{0},\ c_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\Omega) and are a.e. nonnegative, then a unique classical solution to the system (4) exists for all time. Furthermore, the solution is uniformly (with respect to time) bounded in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega).

We use the same entropy entropy dissipation method to obtain an explicit exponential convergence rate for the two species system in any dimension.

Proof.

4 Remarks and open problems

We believe this approach works to prove and quantify the decay rate to the complex balanced equilibrium for more general systems of the type

A1+A2+…+An−1+m​An⇌An+An+1,A_{1}+A_{2}+...+A_{n-1}+mA_{n}{\rightleftharpoons}A_{n}+A_{n+1},

and even more complex systems such as

A1+A2+…+An−1+m​An⇌An+An+1⇋B1+…+Bk+l​An,A_{1}+A_{2}+...+A_{n-1}+mA_{n}{\rightleftharpoons}A_{n}+A_{n+1}{\leftrightharpoons}B_{1}+...+B_{k}+lA_{n},

where k≥1k\geq 1 and l,m≥2l,\ m\geq 2 are integers.

In order to obtain the uniform essential bound on the densities we used the L∞L^{\infty} version of Poincaré’s inequality, which is only available in 1D. Can we employ more refined techniques in order to prove the essential bounds in higher dimensions? These are some questions we plan to address in future work.

which implies

x−yx​y≤ln⁡((xy)).\frac{x-y}{\sqrt{xy}}\leq\ln{\bigg(\frac{x}{y}\bigg)}.

It follows

Ψ⁡(x,y)≥x​(x−y)x​y−x+y=xy​x−x​y−x+y=xy​x+x​y−2​x​y−x+y≥2​x−2​x​y−x+y=(x−y)2.\begin{split}&\Psi{(x,y)}\geq x\frac{(x-y)}{\sqrt{xy}}-x+y=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}x-\sqrt{xy}-x+y\\ &=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}x+\sqrt{xy}-2\sqrt{xy}-x+y\geq 2x-2\sqrt{xy}-x+y=(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{2}.\end{split}

∎

The second important tool is:

Lemma 5.2.

For each fixed y>0y>0,

ψ⁡(x,y):=Ψ⁡(x,y)(x−y)2​ is increasing in ​x∈(0,∞).\psi(x,y):=\frac{\Psi{(x,y)}}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{2}}\mbox{ is increasing in }x\in(0,\infty). (39)
Proof.

Suppose x>y>0x>y>0 and set k=xy>1k=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}>1. We have

dψ⁡(x,y)dx=ln⁡((xy))​(x−y)2−[x​ln⁡((xy))−x+y]​(x−y)​1x(x−y)4=ln⁡((xy))⁡(x−y)−[x​ln⁡((xy))−x+y]​1x(x−y)3=[2​(k−1)​ln⁡k−(2​k​ln⁡(k)−k+1k)]​y(x−y)3=(k−2​ln⁡(k)−1k)​y(x−y)3.\begin{split}&\derivative{\psi{(x,y)}}{x}=\frac{\ln{\big(\frac{x}{y}\big)}(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{2}-\big[x\ln{\big(\frac{x}{y}\big)}-x+y\big]\big(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}\big)\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{4}}\\ &=\frac{\ln{\big(\frac{x}{y}\big)}\big(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}\big)-\big[x\ln{\big(\frac{x}{y}\big)}-x+y\big]\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{3}}\\ &=\frac{\big[2(k-1)\ln k-\big(2k\ln{k}-k+\frac{1}{k}\big)\big]\sqrt{y}}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{3}}=\frac{\big(k-2\ln{k}-\frac{1}{k}\big)\sqrt{y}}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^{3}}.\end{split}

Since we have k>1k>1, we use (38) to obtain

k−1k2​ln⁡(k)=k−1kOPENln⁡(k)−ln⁡((1kCLOSE))≥k⋅1k⟹k−2​ln⁡(k)−1k≥0.\frac{k-\frac{1}{k}}{2\ln{k}}=\frac{k-\frac{1}{k}}{\ln{k}-\ln{(\frac{1}{k}})}\geq\sqrt{k\cdot\frac{1}{k}}\implies k-2\ln{k}-\frac{1}{k}\geq 0.

Combine this with x−y≥0\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}\geq 0 and y>0y>0 to get

dψ⁡(x,y)dx≥0.\derivative{\psi{(x,y)}}{x}\geq 0.

We can use the same way to show this inequality is correct when y>x>0y>x>0. ∎
